amendments.why: Rule 20 already rules that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added`, and names *it was not you that sent me hither* — a clause containing all three words of an English cleft frame. It rules on one of them and leaves the copula and the cleft relative unaddressed, so a verse pass meeting a cleft has to infer two thirds of the answer from the rule's boundary test. JOB.32.9 met it twice in one verse: *It is not the great that are wise, Nor the aged that understand justice*, where three of the chapter's nine `added` units are the frame's pieces, and the verse's own review note records a correction to reach them. The amendment states the whole frame and its limits rather than leaving the silence for the next reader. It narrows nothing: the existing cleft sentence stands unchanged and the new paragraph follows it, deriving the copula from this rule's own *which morpheme is there to carry the English* test and the relative from rule 46's explicit exclusion of a relative supplied over a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent. No corpus row supplied for this chapter bears on English clefts, so nothing contradicts it. The three limits — a written אֲשֶׁר, an explicit pronoun, and a clefted clause that is itself verbless — keep it from reaching cases other rules already own.
amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **And where the ASV clefts a clause, the whole English frame goes the same way.** A cleft writes a dummy *it*, a copula, and a relative before the clause that carries the predication, and where the Hebrew writes a finite verb for that predication no morpheme answers to any of the three: the dummy and its copula are one `added` unit headed on the copula, and the cleft relative is its own `added` unit under rule 55, which marks a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause no written subordinator reaches. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.

conventions: A supplied English relative is `added` where it subordinates a finite clause to a written antecedent, and joins its neighbour's unit where it attaches an anarthrous participle to an antecedent written elsewhere. JOB.32.9 marks both cleft *that*s `added` over the finite יֶחְכָּמוּ and יָבִינוּ, and JOB.32.19 marks *which* `added` over the finite יִפָּתֵחַ after the written יַיִן, while JOB.32.12 keeps *that convinced* and *that answered* whole with their participles, the antecedent *none* being אַיִן's under rule 46's coordinated-substantive rider. What decides it is whether a participle or a finite verb follows, never that the ASV wrote a relative; JOB.32.9's units are a recorded correction from a reading that folded them into the substantival adjectives.

לְיָמִים standing after a predicate adjective leaves both the preposition and יוֹם `unrepresented`: צָעִיר אֲנִי לְיָמִים → *I am young* (JOB.32.6) and זְקֵנִים־הֵמָּה מִמֶּנּוּ לְיָמִים → *they were elder than he* (JOB.32.4). Rule 40's fusion sentence does not reach either, because the explicit pronoun — and at JOB.32.4 the comparative phrase besides — stands between the adjective and the prepositional phrase, so the contiguity that sentence requires fails and rule 2 splits them, as it splits גָּדַל ... מִן → *exceeded*. BSB represents יָמִים at JOB.32.6; that is the convention difference rule 21 describes, not an error.

This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amended.why: Rule 20 already rules that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added`, and names *it was not you that sent me hither* — a clause containing all three words of an English cleft frame. It rules on one of them and leaves the copula and the cleft relative unaddressed, so a verse pass meeting a cleft has to infer two thirds of the answer from the rule's boundary test. JOB.32.9 met it twice in one verse: *It is not the great that are wise, Nor the aged that understand justice*, where three of the chapter's nine `added` units are the frame's pieces, and the verse's own review note records a correction to reach them. The amendment states the whole frame and its limits rather than leaving the silence for the next reader. It narrows nothing: the existing cleft sentence stands unchanged and the new paragraph follows it, deriving the copula from this rule's own *which morpheme is there to carry the English* test and the relative from rule 46's explicit exclusion of a relative supplied over a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent. No corpus row supplied for this chapter bears on English clefts, so nothing contradicts it. The three limits — a written אֲשֶׁר, an explicit pronoun, and a clefted clause that is itself verbless — keep it from reaching cases other rules already own.

report: Checked all 35 candidate lemma groups; every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by the source or by a word the ASV actually wrote, and no split was found. The ones worth naming: הַ at 32.1 (unrepresented, the demonstrative אֵלֶּה taking the phrase's one determiner) against 32.5 (the article taking the supplied *these*, no demonstrative present) is rule 41's own count, exactly הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא. מִן before an infinitive at 32.1 (*to*, the one function word standing in the preposition's slot, rule 52) against 32.6 (*not*, a privative recast as a negative complement, rule 48); 32.22, with no preposition present, correctly gives its *to* to the infinitive under rule 52's closing sentence. מִלָּה at 32.11 (*what to say*, head *say*) against 32.15 (*a word to say*, head *word*) is rule 31's subtraction moving the head because 32.15 writes the noun and 32.11 does not. בֶּטֶן at 32.18 (*within*, a construct relation the ASV recast, rule 19) against 32.19 (*breast*, an absolute noun with its suffix). לְ at 32.10 (*to*) against 32.20 (unrepresented, the dative's object becoming the English subject, rule 40).

Swept the nine `added` units, which the candidate table is blind to. Supplied coordinators with no waw in the clause are `added` three times — *Or* (32.12), *and* (32.16), *Else* (32.22) — and never folded into a neighbouring rendering. Supplied relatives are the chapter's hard case and turn on one criterion: `added` where the relative subordinates a finite clause to a written antecedent (32.9 t006 and t012, over יֶחְכָּמוּ and יָבִינוּ; 32.19 *which*, over יִפָּתֵחַ), kept whole with the substantive where it attaches an anarthrous participle to an antecedent written elsewhere (32.12 *that convinced* and *that answered*, the antecedent *none* being אַיִן's, under rule 46's coordinated-substantive rider). JOB.32.9's review note records this as a correction from an earlier reading, so the chapter reached the criterion rather than assuming it.

The rest of the supplied-English sweep is uniform. Phrasal particles go to their verbs everywhere (*held back* 32.6, *searched out* 32.11, *stand still* 32.16, *take away* 32.22), heads staying on the verb under rule 44. Supplied determiners go to their nominals everywhere (*a spirit* 32.8, *a word* 32.15, *any man's* and *any man* 32.21, and the supplied *the* on construct nouns at 32.2, 32.5, 32.6, 32.8, 32.18). The one supplied possessive with no morpheme behind it is `added` (32.14 *his*), while 32.12's written suffix takes its own *his*. Fused particle pairs head consistently: עַל־כֵּן, עַל אֲשֶׁר and לָכֵן on the opening morpheme under rule 23's second branch, כִּמְעַט on מְעַט under its first, since only there does one morpheme carry a lexeme.

לְיָמִים recurs at 32.4 and 32.6 and is read the same way both times: preposition and noun both `unrepresented`. Rule 40's fusion sentence does not reach either, because the explicit pronoun — and at 32.4 the comparative phrase besides — stands between the predicate adjective and the prepositional phrase, so the contiguity that rule imposes fails and rule 2 splits them. Recorded as a convention, since the fusion reading is tempting and the verse pass would otherwise rederive it.

BSB: no genuine error among the disagreements. The two articles at 32.1 and הִיא at 32.8 are cases the contract rules on explicitly against BSB (rules 41 and 20, the latter forbidding the copula on a tripartite resuming pronoun in so many words). The four prepositions, הֶם at 32.15 and the apodosis waw at 32.5 are the documented convention differences of rules 40, 21 and 14. The Sh at 32.10 and the Sn at 32.11 are rule 32's paragogics, which that rule names as the standing BSB disagreement. יָמִים at 32.6 is the לְיָמִים judgment above. No accepted edge was changed.

Two judgment calls are carried with their alternatives already named in the verse notes and conflict with nothing else in the chapter: *and yet* read as one connective for the single waw at 32.3, and the *not* of *have not* read as part of the recast הֶעְתִּיקוּ at 32.15. Left as accepted.
